c.tagline: Sleepy Mekong capital of gilded stupas, baguettes, and river sunsets.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis are unmetered; agree the fare (or use a fixed airport rate) before riding, or book through the Loca app for set pricing.

emergency.note: Fire: 190. English-speaking dispatch cannot be guaranteed; larger hotels can call on your behalf, and Mahosot Hospital / Alliance International Medical Center are common expat referrals.

avoid.reason: Motorbike bag-snatching and petty theft happen along the riverfront and quiet streets at night; agree tuk-tuk fares in advance.

hood_desc: The compact French-colonial core around the fountain plaza, packed with cafes, bakeries, and boutique hotels; ideal for first-time visitors who want to walk everywhere.
A breezy strip along Fa Ngum Road with sunset bars, the night market, and river views; best for travelers wanting evening atmosphere and riverside dining.
The grand ceremonial boulevard linking the Presidential Palace to the Patuxai monument, lined with government buildings and international-chain hotels; suits business travelers.
A quieter, more spiritual district anchored by the golden Pha That Luang stupa, with wide avenues and fewer tourists; good for those seeking a peaceful base near temples.
The bustling downtown market quarter near the bus terminal and Mekong bridge road, popular with budget travelers and those needing early transit connections.

water.note: Tap water isn't safe even in the capital; drink bottled or filtered water, though commercial ice in tourist spots is usually fine.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (Lao Kip) directly to the conductor on board; there is no rechargeable transit card. Intercity and airport shuttle buses are also cash-only, though some private minivan transfers can be prepaid online.
transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6am-6pm with limited frequency and no reliable night service; tuk-tuks, taxis, or the Loca app fill the gap in the evenings.
transit.note: Public transit is minimal for a capital city; most residents and visitors get around by tuk-tuk, taxi, rented scooter/bicycle, or the Loca ride-hailing app.

train: Thanaleng-Nong Khai cross-border train to Thailand
bus: Talat Sao Bus Station (local & northern routes)

tip.r: Not traditionally expected in Lao culture, but rounding up bills or leaving 5-10% at tourist-oriented restaurants, and tipping tour guides/drivers a few dollars per day, is appreciated.

food.name: Laap
food.desc: The Lao national dish: minced pork, beef, duck or fish tossed with toasted rice powder, lime, chili, mint and herbs. Eaten by hand with sticky rice.

places.name: Pa Kham Tan
places.note: A local spot with a reputation for outstanding laap; simple room, serious cooking.

places.name: Kualao Restaurant
places.note: Colonial villa serving the full Lao canon with nightly traditional dance; a longtime landmark.

places.name: Phakhao Lao
places.note: Modern Lao kitchen focused on traditional recipes and regional ingredients.

food.name: Tam Mak Hoong
food.desc: Lao green papaya salad, pounded in a clay mortar with lime, chili, garlic, tomato, peanuts and padaek fermented fish sauce. Funkier than Thai som tam.

places.name: Chao Anouvong night market stalls
places.note: Pounded to order from 5pm daily; say how many chilies you want before they start.

places.name: Kualao Restaurant
places.note: A milder sit-down version for anyone easing into padaek for the first time.

places.name: Dongpalane Road tam stalls
places.note: Roadside stands where locals buy it to go with sticky rice and grilled chicken.

food.name: Khao Piak Sen
food.desc: Hand-cut fresh rice noodles, thick and chewy like udon, in pork or chicken broth topped with fried garlic and shallots. Breakfast food, gone by mid-morning.

places.name: Khao Piak Pa Bae
places.note: Nearly 40 years old, with chicken or sliced pork; bowls start around 15,000 kip.

places.name: Dongpalane Road noodle shops
places.note: Morning-only stalls cutting the noodles fresh; arrive before 9am for the best of it.

food.name: Ping Kai and Khao Niaw
food.desc: Butterflied chicken marinated in lemongrass, garlic and fish sauce, grilled slowly over charcoal and eaten with baskets of sticky rice and jeow chili dips.

places.name: Chao Anouvong riverside grills
places.note: Charcoal grills fire up at dusk along the promenade; eat with a Beerlao at the water's edge.

places.name: Kualao Restaurant
places.note: Serves ping kai with sticky rice as part of its traditional set menus.

places.name: Khop Chai Deu
places.note: Central old-house restaurant and bar; easy English menu and reliable Lao grill plates.

food.name: Sai Oua
food.desc: Lao herb sausage packed with lemongrass, kaffir lime leaf, galangal and chili, grilled until the skin blisters. Sliced and eaten with sticky rice and greens.

places.name: Kualao Restaurant
places.note: Sai oua is a menu fixture here alongside laap, ping kai and crispy Mekong river weed.

places.name: Phakhao Lao
places.note: Makes its own sausage; a good introduction to the range of Lao charcuterie.

places.name: Night market food stalls
places.note: Sold by the link straight off the grill; the cheapest way to try it.

food.name: Khao Jee Pate
food.desc: The Lao baguette sandwich, a French leftover: crackly bread filled with pate, Lao sausage, pickled carrot, cucumber, herbs and chili sauce.

places.name: Nam Phu Fountain street carts
places.note: Morning sandwich carts around the fountain square, assembled to order in a couple of minutes.

places.name: Kung's Cafe Lao
places.note: Home-cooked Lao food at low prices; a sit-down alternative to the street carts.

food.name: Beerlao
food.desc: The national lager, brewed with local jasmine rice since 1973. Sold in big bottles poured over ice, and an institution in its own right.

places.name: Kong View
places.note: Riverside restaurant with sunset views over the Mekong; a classic first-night Beerlao stop.

places.name: Khop Chai Deu
places.note: Long-running garden bar in the old town, busy from early evening onwards.

places.name: Chao Anouvong Park riverfront
places.note: Plastic tables along the promenade where locals drink and watch the sun go down.

food.name: Lao Coffee
food.desc: Robusta grown on the Bolaven Plateau, brewed dark through a cloth sock and served over condensed milk and ice. Thick, sweet and very strong.

places.name: Kung's Cafe Lao
places.note: Praised for unusual and very tasty coffees at low prices; also a good breakfast stop.

places.name: Nam Phu area cafes
places.note: Cluster of cafes near the fountain roasting Bolaven beans; good for a sit-down iced coffee.

landmarks: Pha That Luang
This gold-covered Buddhist stupa is Laos's most sacred monument and national symbol, its gleaming tiered spire dominating the city skyline and appearing on the national emblem.
Patuxai (Victory Gate)
Resembling a Lao twist on Paris's Arc de Triomphe, this ornate war memorial arch lets visitors climb to a rooftop terrace with panoramic views down Vientiane's grand avenue.
Wat Si Saket
Vientiane's oldest surviving temple stuns visitors with cloistered walls containing thousands of tiny Buddha niches, a serene highlight of Lao Buddhist architecture.
Haw Phra Kaew
Once home to the revered Emerald Buddha before it was taken to Bangkok, this former royal temple now serves as a museum showcasing exquisite Lao and Khmer religious art.
Wat Si Muang
Believed to house the city's guardian spirit pillar, this vibrant, incense-filled temple is where locals come daily to pray, making it a lively spot to witness living Lao Buddhism.
Presidential Palace
This grand French colonial-style building at the end of Lane Xang Avenue serves as the official residence for state ceremonies, its neoclassical facade a striking city centerpiece.
Wat Ong Teu Mahawihan
Home to one of the country's largest bronze Buddha statues and a prestigious Buddhist monastic school, this temple's intricately carved doors are a highlight for visitors.
Talat Sao (Morning Market)
This sprawling indoor market is where locals shop for textiles, silver jewelry, and street food, offering an authentic, colorful window into everyday Vientiane life.
Mekong River Waterfront
The riverside promenade facing Thailand across the Mekong comes alive each evening with a night market and food stalls, best known for its spectacular fiery sunsets.
COPE Visitor Centre
A free exhibition documenting the impact of unexploded wartime ordnance on Laos, with survivor stories, prosthetics displays, and a giant bomb-casing sculpture out front.

train.note: Two different stations: fast Laos-China Railway trains (Vientiane to Luang Prabang, Boten and direct daytime D887/D888 to Kunming, China) use Vientiane Railway Station north of town, booked via the official 'LCR Ticket' app or at station counters. The overnight direct sleeper to Bangkok uses the separate Khamsavath (Vientiane) station and is sold by State Railway of Thailand. Passport needed for both border crossings.

intl.to: Nong Khai & Udon Thani (Thailand) - across the Friendship Bridge
intl.op: Central and Southern bus station operators — tickets at the terminals, no online booking

intl.to: Hanoi, Hue & Da Nang (Vietnam) - long-distance sleeper coaches
intl.op: Lao and Vietnamese operators — tickets at the terminals or through local agents

bus.note: No branded coach line with online booking. International buses run from the Southern and Central bus stations across the Friendship Bridge to Nong Khai and Udon Thani (Thailand), and long-distance coaches go to Hanoi, Hue and Da Nang (Vietnam). Buy tickets at the terminals or through local agents.

ferry.note: No scheduled international ferry from Vientiane; the Thai border here is crossed by bridge, not boat. Mekong slow boats (e.g. Huay Xai to Luang Prabang) are domestic and start well upriver, not in Vientiane.

half.name: Buddha Park (Xieng Khuan)
half.blurb: A whimsical riverside meadow crowded with towering concrete Buddhas and Hindu deities beside the Mekong.

half.name: Nam Ngum Dam & Reservoir
half.blurb: A vast tranquil reservoir dotted with green islets, ideal for boat rides and lakeside lunches.

half.name: Phou Khao Khouay National Park
half.blurb: A protected upland forest laced with jungle trails, sandstone cliffs and refreshing hidden waterfalls.

half.name: Nong Khai
half.blurb: Just over the Friendship Bridge, this Thai riverside town features the surreal Sala Keoku sculpture park.

half.name: Ban Keun (Lao National Zoo)
half.blurb: A rural riverside village with a sprawling wildlife zoo set among wooded hills and farmland.

full.name: Vang Vieng
full.blurb: A backpacker haven cradled by dramatic karst peaks, blue lagoons, caves and lazy river tubing.

laundry.note: Local shops about 25,000 kip per kilo, far cheaper than hotels

Large gym with a full boxing ring inside the ITECC complex. A separate source (roampads.com) cites 80,000 kip, so treat as approximate.
